newsitem.title: UK: Europe relieved but saddened as Peru crisis ends.
newsitem.headline: Europe relieved but saddened as Peru crisis ends.

text.p: European nations on Wednesday greeted the end of the Peru hostage siege with relief tinged by regret at the loss of life in the military operation which climaxed the four-month drama.
A contingent of 140 Peruvian commandos stormed the beseiged Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima in a surprise assault on Tuesday and rescued 71 hostages.
One hostage -- a Peruvian Supreme Court judge -- and two commandos died and all 14 Marxist rebels were killed, although four had apparently tried to surrender.

Britain, France, Germany and Spain welcomed the freeing of the hostages as good news for their families and for the diplomatic community but all expressed sadness over the deaths of the two soldiers and the judge.
Russia, which has shown itself in the past more inclined to end hostage dramas through force rather than negotiation, applauded the "skilful and cool-headed operation.
"The end of the operation...was viewed with satisfaction and relief," the foreign ministry said in a statement.

Spain, which has close ties to the Latin American country and has been in constant contact with its Lima embassy throughout the crisis, was the most guarded in its reaction to the storming of the residence.
Deputy Prime Minister Francisco Alvarez Cascos told reporters: "The result of the assault, in that it has meant there were a certain number of victims, cannot be viewed with satisfaction.
"The liberation of the hostages is good news for their families and the diplomatic community, but it is tarnished by the existence of victims."
There were three Spaniards among the initial 500 hostages taken when the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement rebels seized the residence. They were freed early on.
France said the military assault put an end to an intolerable 126-day ordeal whose responsibility fell only upon the hostage-takers.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said the Tupac Amaru guerrillas had used inexcusable terrorist methods condemned throughout the world.
"One can only be relieved that those who went through this ordeal recovered their freedom, and we assure them of our sympathy," he told a news briefing.
Britain congratulated the Peruvian government on the ending of the crisis and said it showed that international cooperation was the key to success.
"We congratulate the Peruvian government on last night's successful rescue operation which has brought this long-running incident to an end," the Foreign Office said.

Media reports said British security forces, including members of the SAS elite unit, played a vital role in the rescue and had been on standby throughout the four-month drama. British hostage negotiators were also involved, the reports said.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel sent his Peruvian counterpart a telegram expressing his relief at the successful end to the drama.
"Our thoughts are with those innocent people who have fallen victim to this barbaric hostage taking," Kinkel wrote in the telegram.
The Vatican echoed his sentiments: "The loss of human life is always a source of pain for all," chief spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said in a statement.
